A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SONAR research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original SONAR benchmark results, architectural ablations, embedding analyses, bandwidth sensitivity and inference measurements.

after.justification: V2 retains original SONAR results and adds high-frequency probing, shared-encoder ablation, neural-codec evaluation and computational measurements.

M1.justification: The principal architecture, SRM constraints, cross-attention and JS/WCE objective remain unchanged. However, v1 Sections 4.4 and 5.1 explicitly update the final two Mamba layers during finetuning, whereas v2 Section 4.3 says only the noise path and fusion layers are updated. This is a limited change in the reported training procedure; it does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: ASVspoof 2019 training and ASVspoof 2021 LA/DF and In-the-Wild evaluation remain. V2 adds two input scenarios on In-the-Wild: audio retaining only frequencies above 4 kHz and audio re-encoded through the Descript Audio Codec. No new corpus, language or modality is evaluated.

E2.justification: All seven principal comparators in Table 1 are retained. Computational evaluation expands beyond the existing XLSR-Mamba latency comparison to an explicitly measured single-encoder XLSR+AASIST comparator in v2 Table 3 and Appendix G.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands the diagnostic evaluation design: logistic-regression probes on pooled high-pass embeddings report EER, AUC and accuracy at EER; zero-shot DAC evaluation adds AUC and score-rank correlation; and a new computational benchmark measures parameters, FLOPs and latency. The principal dataset splits and benchmark EER protocol remain. The probe training/evaluation split is unspecified.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of high-frequency representation quality, encoder-weight sharing and resilience to neural-codec resynthesis, plus quantitative computational analysis. These address substantive mechanism, architectural and robustness questions. V1's t-SNE comparison is removed, while its cosine-similarity analysis and bandwidth sweep are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report three independent SONAR runs, best and mean results in Table 1, and identical ITW significance tests: t=19.4, p=0.0026 and t=4.73, p=0.0419. V2 introduces no additional uncertainty-reporting or significance-testing procedure for its new analyses.

E6.justification: Table 1 is numerically unchanged, but substantial new results appear. V2's probes report baseline/SONAR EERs of 32.51/26.57 for XLSR-AASIST and 29.77/26.08 for XLSR-Mamba. DAC processing changes SONAR-Full's ITW EER from 6.00% to 8.60% and AUC from 0.977 to 0.953. Shared-weight ablation and computational measurements are added, and Table 2 replaces qualitative codec-output shifts with explicit values. These are additional findings, not improved scores on the retained main benchmark.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces v1's approximate LF-HF independence assumption for fakes and claimed Pinsker-derived Bayes-error bound with a hypothesis that HF distributions conditioned on LF differ between classes. V2 adds complementary projection definitions and Fourier-derivative reasoning, and explicitly treats JS alignment as a bounded surrogate rather than an estimator of conditional dependence.

C1.justification: The central SONAR, generalization, SOTA and fast-convergence claims persist. V2 drops the explicit claim of disjoint real/fake latent manifolds in favor of LF-HF consistency, and revises the contribution list to emphasize empirical diagnosis of spectral bias in existing detectors.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking probe results to a high-frequency blind spot, shared-weight degradation to differing content/noise distributions, and performance gains to representation learning rather than capacity alone. It interprets DAC results as evidence that alignment cues survive neural resynthesis. Bandwidth sensitivity is now also framed as positive mechanistic evidence, and bandwidth-matched finetuning is said to restore accuracy without supporting results. The original deployment limitations largely remain in Appendix D.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a public repository reference for code/checkpoints and a demo instead of v1's acceptance-dependent release and supplementary-access statements; external availability was not verified. It clarifies linear 1x1 residual mixing and identifies calflops and the Quadro RTX 8000 profiling hardware. Conversely, it omits previously stated details including 64,600-sample clips, cosine annealing and three-epoch early-stopping patience.

R1.justification: The core positioning against SRM, dual-stream and self-supervised detectors remains. V2 adds Kumar et al. for the neural codec and removes peripheral references, including Maltby's frequency-bin analysis and RawBMamba. Several retained references receive publication or bibliographic updates, which do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, motivation, experimental discussion and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Lite and Finetune are combined into one subsection; the appendix is organized into Sections A-G; impact discussion moves into the main text; and a conflict-of-interest disclosure is added.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout and extensively resizes and rearranges figures and tables. It adds probe ROC and neural-codec plots plus computational and probing tables, removes the t-SNE panel, and redraws the retained cosine-similarity display. The latency figure moves from the appendix into the main text; the bandwidth plot and licensing tables are retained under new numbering.

improvement.justification: V2 replaces the unsupported Bayes-error guarantee with a more qualified modeling hypothesis and adds useful architectural, spectral-probing and neural-codec evidence. Explicit code-access and computational information also improve transparency. These gains are limited by unspecified probe splits, omitted training details and unreconciled efficiency prose: Table 3 reports latency increasing from 29.0 to 57.3 ms despite the nearby claim that it does not approximately double.
